$comment: The LinkedIn channel bible. It inherits the show's register from series.json - promise, invites, avoids, avoid_patterns are all enforced against post copy by validate.py - and adds only what is specific to publishing on a feed: the mechanics of the fold, the shape of a post, and the rules that keep the account from sounding like marketing.

cadence.note: One a week that is genuinely good beats two that are filler. Move to two only when the queue holds at least four ready posts, so a slow week never forces a weak one.
cadence.scan_rhythm: One scouring pass a week against data/linkedin/sources.json. A pass that finds nothing publishable is a normal outcome and is not a reason to lower the bar.

audience.$comment: Same person as the podcast listener, arriving through a different door and giving you two seconds instead of forty minutes.
audience.who: A manager or senior practitioner responsible for delivery in any field. They have been handed software configured by someone who has never done their job.
audience.what_they_are_doing_when_they_see_it: Scrolling between meetings, on a phone, deciding in under two seconds whether to tap 'see more'.
audience.why_they_stop: They recognise their own working week in the first line. Recognition, not novelty, is what earns the tap.
audience.what_makes_them_leave: Being sold to, being told they are behind, or reading a paragraph that could have been written by someone who has never run anything.

mechanics.$comment: Platform facts the copy has to survive. Numbers here are enforced by validate.py.
mechanics.line_length: Short paragraphs, one to three lines. A wall of text on a phone is a scroll.
mechanics.links: No external link in the body - put it in the first comment and say so in the post. A body link costs reach and the post has to stand alone anyway.

hashtags.note: At the end, never mid-sentence. They are filing labels, not decoration.

mechanics.$long_form: A post may declare "long_form": true when the argument genuinely needs the room - a flagship the account expects to point back to. It is then checked against long_form_max_chars instead of the target range, which still leaves headroom under the platform limit for a late edit. Rare by design: if every post is long form, none of them is.

shape.$comment: The four parts of every post in this repo. The close is a real question, not engagement bait - see 'avoids'.
shape.hook: One or two lines that fit above the fold. It names a situation the reader has been in, or states the claim flat. It never teases the payoff.
shape.body: The argument, in short paragraphs. At least one concrete, checkable specific - a threshold, a sentence someone would actually say, a step in a process.
shape.close: A question they can answer from their own week without disclosing anything they would regret. It has to be a question you would genuinely want the answer to.

formats.$comment: Controlled vocabulary for a post's 'format' field.
formats.argument: A claim, the reasoning, and what follows from it. The default.
formats.reframe: Takes a thing the reader already believes and turns it ninety degrees. Strongest format this account has, because the show's whole premise is a reframe.
formats.field-note: One concrete thing observed or reported, told small and specific, with the general point left implicit until the last line.
formats.playbook: A short numbered or bulleted procedure someone could run on Monday. Use sparingly - it invites skimming.
formats.question: Opens a real question the author has not settled, and says so. Only honest if it is true.

voice.$comment: series.json 'voice' governs here in full. These are the additions that only bite on a feed.
invites: Lead with the reader's situation, not with the technology. The first line should be recognisable to someone who has never touched an agent.
One concrete specific per post - a dollar threshold, a sentence somebody said, a step in a process. Abstraction is what makes a post forgettable.
Say the claim flat. A hook that teases ('the reason will surprise you') spends trust the account has to keep.
Write so that a reader who thinks the whole thing is oversold can still finish it and disagree with something specific.
Attribute honestly. Reported is reported, and a framework is somebody's framework.

Say 'AI agent' the first time, in every post. On a feed the reader does not expand 'agent' into 'AI agent' - they read a person, a booking agent, an insurance agent. Once it is labelled, 'agents' is fine for the rest of the post.
avoids: Engagement bait. 'Agree?', 'Thoughts?', 'Comment YES below', the fake poll. It works once and costs the account its register.
The broetry cadence - every sentence its own paragraph for drama. Short paragraphs, not one-line theatre.
Statistics without a checked citation. See 'statistics' below.
Prediction as content. Nobody needs another take on what AI will do to work by 2030; the account's material is what people already did last Tuesday.
Naming a vendor as the hero, including the ones this account likes.
Recycled hook formulas. 'I asked AI to X and the result shocked me' is not this account.
voice.statistics: No number goes in a post unless the nugget it comes from carries citation_status 'verified' and a source you have actually opened. Structural arguments do not need the number to work, and a wrong number is the one mistake this audience will remember.

avoid_patterns.$comment: Case-insensitive substrings validate.py flags in post copy, on top of the show-wide list in series.json. These are the feed-specific failures: engagement bait, hook formulas, and the vocabulary of a vendor.
avoid_patterns.agree?: Engagement bait. Ask something you actually want the answer to.
avoid_patterns.thoughts?: Engagement bait. A real question names what you are asking about.
avoid_patterns.will shock you: Hook formula. Say the claim flat.
avoid_patterns.will surprise you: Hook formula. Say the claim flat.
avoid_patterns.the future of work is here: Prediction as content, and a cliche.

do_not_post: Anything that reads as a vendor case study, including the ones with real results.
Client or employer specifics that were not offered publicly by the person they belong to.
A response to a news item within a day of it breaking, before the facts settle.
A post whose only content is that a model was released.

measurement.$comment: What to watch, so the account does not get optimised into slop.
measurement.primary: Comments from people who do the work, describing their own version of the thing. That is the signal the register is landing.
measurement.secondary: Saves and DMs. Both mean it was useful rather than agreeable.
measurement.ignore: Impressions on a post that got them by being provocative. Reach bought that way selects for an audience this account does not want.
measurement.review: Once a quarter, read the ten posts with the most practitioner comments and ask what they had in common. Feed that back into the formats, not into the hooks.

citation_status.$comment: How much weight a nugget's claim can carry in public. validate.py enforces these values on every nugget.
citation_status.verified: You have opened the primary source yourself. The only status that permits a number in a post.
citation_status.reported: Somebody reported it, and the report is identifiable. Say who, and say reported.
citation_status.attributed: It is a named framework or argument rather than a finding. Attribute it as such.
citation_status.framing: A way of seeing the thing, owned by this account. Nothing to cite, and nothing to claim as evidence.

spine_gaps_accepted.$comment: Spine themes the current queue does not carry. The feed is supposed to say all four over time, so validate.py fails on an uncovered theme unless it is declared here - the exception stays visible in the data rather than quietly disappearing when posts get cut. Each entry says what would close it.
spine_gaps_accepted.customization-as-superpower: Left uncovered when the rent-versus-own and tackle-box posts were cut. The material is still in the nuggets - nug-rent-vs-own, nug-tackle-box, nug-capability-escalator - so the way to close this is one post on turnkey software never having been turnkey, and the team's workarounds being the specification all along.

identity.$comment: The account's own names. The subscribe line and the first comment are assembled from these, so they change in one place. A field left empty is a channel the show does not use yet - nothing references it, and validate.py only complains when a rendered post or first comment shows a [[placeholder]] because something referenced it anyway.

cta.$comment: The subscribe line, appended to every post at render time. It lives here rather than in each post so it changes in one place and stays consistent, and it is short on purpose - it is the toll for the post, not the point of it.
cta.placement: After the close question, before the hashtags. Never above the fold, and never in place of the question - a post that ends on a pitch instead of a question gets no comments.
cta.link_policy: The body carries no link at all. An external link in the body costs reach, and a scroller between meetings will not leave the feed for one - but they will follow, which is a tap. The episode link goes in the first comment, where the people who tapped through are the ones who wanted it. Switch the cta variant to 'page' once there is a LinkedIn Page to follow.

variants.default: We turn these arguments into interviews with the people who run the work. Follow along here for the posts, and {show_name} is on YouTube - link in the first comment.
variants.page: We turn these arguments into interviews with the people who run the work. Follow {linkedin_page} for the posts, and {show_name} is on YouTube - link in the first comment.
variants.short: {show_name} is interviews with people who run the work, in their own words. Episode link in the first comment.

first_comment.$comment: The first comment is assembled rather than written per post: a fixed lead carrying the episode link, then whatever sourcing note the post declares in its own first_comment field. Every post gets one, so the link is never forgotten on the posts nobody spent an evening on.
first_comment.lead: {show_name} is the podcast behind these posts - conversations with people who run the work, about how they actually run it. Episodes on YouTube: {youtube_url}
first_comment.timing: Post it yourself within a minute of publishing, from the same account. A first comment that arrives an hour later is a comment nobody scrolled back for.
